newsitem.title: FRANCE: Sorry saga of French bank Credit Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: Sorry saga of French bank Credit Lyonnais.

text.p: The sorry saga of the French state bank Credit Lyonnais reads like the script of a movie that could well have been made by the Hollywood studios which it owned in its heyday.

News that the government is coming to its financial rescue for the third year in a row is undoubtedly a relief -- but also humbling for a bank nationalised by President Charles de Gaulle to underpin French economic recovery after World War Two.

In the space of five years, the bank has fallen with a thud from the dizzy heights of 1980s and turned in losses in the tens of billions of francs. Politicians and technocrats fought over who to blame and, to crown it, the Paris headquarters burnt down.
Things went badly awry in the 1990s when many of the huge investments, acquisitions and loans that made it the biggest bank outside Japan turned sour.

The bill was a staggering loss of 21 billion francs ($4.1 billion) between 1992 and 1994, the forced exit of the former chairman Jean-Yves Haberer and the start of several, highly costly and complicated government attempts to put the bank back on its feet.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis has also asked for an inquiry to establish who precisely was to blame and whether company law should be revised to enlarge on legal liability for company accounts.

Some also see the inquiry as a clever political manoeuvre to pursue Haberer, who was appointed in 1988 under late Socialist President Francois Mitterrand, at a time when the current centre-right ruling coalition is mired in a series of probes into political party funding and housing scandals.
One of the debacles that pushed Credit Lyonnais to the brink of ruin was a $1.0 billion loan to Italian businessmen Giancarlo Paretti and Florio Fiorini to buy the Metro Goldwyn Mayer film studios.
The bank inherited the studios after they went bankrupt and now been sold off under a divestment programme which is part of a government rescue package put into action last year.

That package was the second in two years but a third rescue is now under preparation because the complex financing of the 1995 rescue plan that was supposed to help the bank is actually draining money away from it.

This year alone the bank is expected to lose three billion francs on a shortfall between the interest payments it gets from a separate holding company which is selling off its assets and the interest rates it is paying on the money it lent to the holding company to carry out the sell-off programme.

An emergency government aid of 3.9 billion francs passed the hurdle of European Commission approval on Wednesday and is designed to alleviate the pain while the French finance ministry works on what will undoubtedly by a far more costly cure.
The EU authorities put an estimate of 45 billion francs on the cost of the 1995 rescue alone and details of the third plan have yet to emerge.
If the film-makers are interested, there are plenty of other spicy bits for a movie.
The bank's 19th century headquarters, whose architect drew inspiration from the Louvre museum, was gutted in May.

And another of its most celebrated clients is himself in the movies. Credit Lyonnais financed the rags-to-riches career of former businessman, soccer boss and politician Bernard Tapie -- now the star of the movie "Men, Women: Instructions for use". ($1=5.101 French Franc)
